title: Dance on Freeman's place beside Lester Young
summary: Dance says Freeman was the only white tenor of his kind in Chicago and hears a family relationship with Lester Young.

story.theme_name: Lester Young: the man, the sound, the Basie years
story.community_name: Remembering Lester Young: Prez the man and his sound

blocks.x: But, on the subject of Lester, It's funny, I told you I was a fan of yours long before I met you. When I was still in Chicago, and really before you had become any sort of a household name. What you were doing meant a great deal to me and I was a close friend of Jess Stacy's and you know, you were filling a role there that nobody else was filling. And, as a matter of fact, you were the only white musician I think we can say, perhaps, tenor saxophone player, that was blowing like that.

I don't think -- not that I can think of were there white tenor saxophone players in that category. Of course, plenty they came later, one way or another. Bud, you had have something special which I always heard right from the beginning, and when Lester came along, now, I couldn't say and you'll tell me about, you know, what Lester -- perhaps, what relationship the two of you had together or how much Lester may have heard you and when and how much you heard Lester, but I always heard something and the people admired you very much.

But I always felt that I was hearing something that other people weren't putting their finger on the same way. They all liked it, but I heard something else there. And later, of course, as people realized what Lester was

doing too, and loving Lester. Like, For instance, how Billie Holiday, above everybody, Billie interpreted Lester, particularly felt what he was doing. But it was something unique and different and in after years, as one hears the various records it becomes clear that there is a relationship between you two and I am not talking about one playing like another and or one having heard the other, but it's you might say in the same family.
